plate.alt: Harriet Tubman stands in a rowboat on the Combahee River at night, singing to families hurrying aboard while Union gunboats wait in the moonlight.
plate.credit: The Combahee River Raid, June 1863, the night all three sources describe.

a.raw: the freed families carried babies bundles and chickens onto the waiting steamboats
a.fixed: The freed families carried babies, bundles, and chickens onto the waiting steamboats.
a.why: Capital T starts the sentence; commas separate babies, bundles, and chickens; a period ends it.

b.raw: the scouts watched the river the woods and the roads for rebel guards
b.fixed: The scouts watched the river, the woods, and the roads for Rebel guards.
b.why: Capital T starts the sentence; commas separate the river, the woods, and the roads; capital R on Rebel, the way Sterling writes it; a period ends it.

vocab: Brave and heroic, especially in a noble cause.
A place where food and supplies are stored, especially for an army.
The Confederate states; the land of the rebellion.
During the Civil War, enslaved people who escaped to Union lines.
notes.wordParts: Prefixes that tell where: trans- = across, inter- = between, sub- = under, super- = above or beyond: transportation, international, submarine, supernatural.
notes.grammar: Commas in a series: put a comma after each item in a list of three or more, including before and. She packed bread, cheese, and a knife.
notes.spelling: Some words sound alike but mean different things. Affect is the action, effect is the result. It’s means it is; its shows belonging. Their means belonging to them, there is a place, they’re means they are. Accept means take; except means leave out.

read.label: Marcus · before you read the sources

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Today a third writer joins the story: Sarah Bradford, who wrote a book about Harriet six years after the raid. Today’s question: when writers tell the same story differently, what can the differences teach us?
transcripts.read: Pick one fact, like how many people were freed, or what each writer calls Harriet. Find it in every source and set the versions side by side. Some gaps are small. Some change the whole picture. Read the table straight across, one row at a time.
transcripts.grammar: A list needs commas so the reader can tell where one thing stops and the next begins. Lanterns, quilts, and dried meat. Without commas, you might wonder what a quilt meat is. Put a comma after every item but the last, and keep the one before and.

virtue.title: Moving freedom forward, or holding it back?
virtue.intro: These moments come from this week’s sources and Chapter 18. Tap Moves freedom forward or Holds it back.

items.t: Harriet guides the gunboats past the torpedoes hidden in the river.
items.why: Her scouting keeps the boats safe so they can reach the people waiting on the banks.

items.t: The Rebels hide torpedoes in the river to sink Union boats.
items.why: The torpedoes were set to stop the boats before anyone could be freed.

items.t: A newspaper prints the story but leaves out Harriet’s name.
items.why: Her work is real, but she gets no credit for it.

items.t: Harriet tells her own account, and it is printed in The Commonwealth.
items.why: Her own words reach readers, so the story is told by the person who led it.

items.t: Nearly all the able-bodied men who were freed join the Black regiments.
items.why: People who were just freed fight to free others. (Bradford reprints this from 1863.)
